back: The activity of drawing out information from stakeholders and other sources.
Gathering implies the information is ready to hand over. Stakeholders often cannot express their needs until helped.
Determine elicitation approach; prepare for elicitation; conduct elicitation; confirm elicitation results.

front: How do elicitation and analysis relate?
back: They alternate. Analysis raises new questions, which need more elicitation.

front: When does the elicit-analyze cycle stop?
back: When analysis raises no more questions, or the risk of incomplete information is acceptable.
How elicitation will be done: what information, where it is, how to obtain it, and when. Called an elicitation plan in formal life cycles.
Rework and product defects later.

front: Six steps to prepare for an elicitation activity
back: Determine the objective; determine the participants; identify the resources; identify the questions; set the agenda; schedule the activity.
Items made to help the activity meet its objective: agenda, questions, ground rules, presentation material, models.

front: Three stages of an elicitation activity
back: Introduction, body, close. Follow-up then confirms the results.
Open-ended: can be answered in any way. Closed-ended: the answer comes from a limited list of choices.
Contextual: about the subject at hand. Context-free: could be asked in any situation.
A facilitated group technique for listing many ideas in a short time.
Studying existing documents for relevant product information. Objective, but the documents may be out of date.
A structured meeting led by a skilled, neutral facilitator with selected stakeholders. Fast, and good for reconciling differences.
A facilitated workshop that brings cross-functional stakeholders together to define product information.
Prequalified stakeholders and experts share expectations and attitudes about a proposed solution. Risk: group pressure.
A formal or informal approach of asking prepared or spontaneous questions and recording the answers, usually one to one.
Structured: a prepared list, all asked. Unstructured: only the first question is fixed; the rest follow the answers.
Watching people do their work in their own environment. Also called job shadowing.
People may act differently when they are being observed.
Getting early feedback by showing a model of the expected solution before building it.
Storyboard: images showing sequence or navigation. Wireframe: a static blueprint of a screen. Evolutionary: the real solution in progress.
Written questions for many respondents. Reach a large, dispersed group at low cost. Concern: response rate.
Elicitation techniques that use game play to encourage participation, creativity and collaboration.
Teams design the product's packaging, showing which benefits and features customers value most.
Problems are written on anchors holding back a boat. A non-confrontational way to find what users dislike.
A game that draws the relationships between the product and other products.
The information captured in an elicitation activity, before participants have agreed it is accurate.
Results the product team agrees are accurate, after review with stakeholders.
A peer review in which the author leads the reviewers through the material.

front: Why use a glossary when confirming results?
back: To agree what terms mean and to find terms that different groups use differently.

front: How many sources for each topic?
back: At least two, so no requirement rests on a single opinion or an outdated document.
Predictive: mostly up front, comprehensive, documented. Adaptive: every iteration, just enough, one to two iterations ahead.
A facilitated workshop.

front: Best technique: users cannot picture the solution
back: A prototype.
